check.x: Professionalism
Introduces self to Mrs Costa and her husband as a medical student, and gains consent before assisting and examining.
Stays within the student role: works with the midwife and leaves decisions to the registrar rather than acting alone.
Uses a calm voice, explains each action to Mrs Costa as it is done, and offers support to her husband.
History
Establishes the labour and the change from the midwife:

kids.x: Induction at 39+4 on an oxytocin infusion, with the rate recently increased
Artificial rupture of membranes 20 minutes ago with the head high, at station -2
Epidural top-up 15 minutes ago, and the blood pressure before it
When the CTG changed, and that the contractions have become very frequent

check.x: Asks about constant pain, vaginal bleeding and the colour of the fluid [none, none, clear], to screen for abruption, uterine rupture and meconium.
Past obstetric and medical history: previous vaginal birth, no uterine scar, GBS status, allergies and when she last ate.
Asks Mrs Costa how she feels and acknowledges her worry.
Examination

Looks at the woman, the infusions and the monitor, and checks the signal [good, no loss of contact], saying the transducer would be repositioned or a fetal scalp electrode used if the signal were poor.
Checks maternal observations: pulse, BP [84/50 after the top-up], temperature [37.1 °C] and SpO2, saying a sepsis screen would follow a temperature of 38 °C or above.
Palpates the contractions for frequency, length and relaxation [6 in 10 minutes, about 90 seconds, tense between].
Palpates the abdomen for lie, presentation, engagement and tenderness [longitudinal, cephalic, head 3/5 palpable, non-tender].
Requests or performs a vaginal examination, with consent, to exclude cord prolapse.
Identifies the pulsating cord below the presenting part on vaginal examination.
Interpretation
Describes the CTG as abnormal: a prolonged deceleration to 70 bpm lasting 3 minutes from a baseline of 140 bpm with normal variability, with only a slow partial recovery to 100 bpm.
Identifies tachysystole: 6 contractions in 10 minutes (more than 5) on oxytocin, with poor relaxation between them.
Recognises maternal hypotension (84/50) after the epidural top-up as a contributing cause.
Diagnoses umbilical cord prolapse, with artificial rupture of membranes and a high presenting part as the risk factors, and states that birth must be expedited.
Explains LOA and station:

kids.x: Left, Occiput (the denominator in a vertex presentation), Anterior: the occiput lies towards the left and front of the maternal pelvis
Position is the relationship of the denominator to the maternal pelvis; station -2 means the head is 2 cm above the ischial spines

check.x: Management
Calls for help immediately (midwife in charge, registrar, obstetric emergency call), alongside the first measures.
Stops the oxytocin infusion straight away.
Considers acute tocolysis (terbutaline 250 micrograms subcutaneously) as an adjunct if contractions continue, without letting it delay birth.
Relieves cord compression by elevating the presenting part with gloved fingers, keeping the fingers in place until birth.
Positions her knee-chest or left lateral head-down.
Handles the cord as little as possible to avoid vasospasm, and mentions bladder filling (500 to 750 mL) only if birth will be delayed or transfer is needed.
Corrects the hypotension with an IV fluid bolus and asks for anaesthetic review for a vasopressor if needed.
Asks for a category 1 caesarean through the registrar and prepares for theatre (anaesthetist, theatre, neonatal team, IV access, bloods), stating that no step may delay birth.

Explains to Mrs Costa in plain language that the baby's heart rate has dropped because the cord has slipped down ahead of the baby, why she must change position, and that an urgent caesarean is the safest way to birth the baby; checks understanding and offers for her husband to come to theatre if possible.
Safety netting
After the birth: the neonatal team at the birth, paired cord blood gases, and a debrief with Mrs Costa and her husband before discharge.

Gives warning signs after a caesarean in plain words (heavy bleeding, fever, a red or leaking wound, worsening tummy pain, calf pain or breathlessness) and to contact the birth suite or call 000, with GP follow-up and a plan for the next birth.

desc: This station involves a rapid focused history and examination of a woman in induced labour whose CTG has changed, then interpreting the CTG, her observations and a reassessment, managing umbilical cord prolapse with tachysystole and maternal hypotension as a student working with the midwife, and explaining to the woman what is happening.
explain:
Abnormal CTG: the first steps

An abnormal CTG in labour is a trigger for early help, together with a short set of simple measures: change the woman's position, check and correct maternal hypotension, stop oxytocin or other uterotonics if hyperstimulation is suspected (and consider tocolysis), check temperature (sepsis screen if 38 °C or above), check the signal (reposition the transducer or apply a fetal scalp electrode), and perform a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse. If the trace remains abnormal, fetal scalp stimulation or fetal blood sampling can be considered, or birth expedited; a prolonged deceleration that does not recover needs birth expedited, not fetal blood sampling.

Interpreting the results

The trace had a normal baseline of 140 bpm with normal variability, then a prolonged deceleration to 70 bpm for 3 minutes with only a slow partial recovery to 100 bpm. There are 6 contractions in 10 minutes (tachysystole is more than 5 in 10) on an oxytocin infusion that was recently increased, and her BP has fallen to 84/50 after an epidural top-up. Tachysystole and hypotension both reduce placental blood flow, but the pulsating cord below a high presenting part soon after artificial rupture of the membranes is the cause that matters most: the cord is being compressed, and birth must be expedited.

Umbilical cord prolapse

Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency, with risk factors including a high or unengaged presenting part, malpresentation, polyhydramnios, prematurity and recent artificial rupture of membranes. The cord is compressed between the presenting part and the pelvis, and may also go into vasospasm if handled. Management is:

  • Call for help immediately and assess the fetal heart rate.
  • Relieve cord compression by elevating the presenting part with gloved fingers. If birth will be delayed (for example during transfer), fill the bladder.
  • Position the woman knee-chest or left lateral head-down.
  • Handle the cord as little as possible.
  • Consider acute tocolysis only as an adjunct, for example while contracting or if birth will be delayed.
  • Prepare for birth. None of these steps may delay it. Before full dilatation it is by category 1 caesarean, aiming for birth as fast as is safely possible (generally within 30 minutes); a vaginal or assisted birth is an option only if she is fully dilated and birth can be quick and safe.

After the birth

The neonatal team attends the birth, paired cord blood gases are taken, and the woman and her partner are offered a debrief. Before discharge she is told the warning signs after a caesarean (heavy bleeding, fever, a red or leaking wound, worsening abdominal pain, calf pain or breathlessness) and where to go, with GP follow-up and a discussion of options for her next birth.

Fetal position and station

Position is the relationship of the denominator (the occiput in a vertex presentation) to the maternal pelvis. LOA means the occiput lies towards the left and front of the maternal pelvis, the most common and favourable position for birth. Station is the level of the presenting part relative to the ischial spines, so station -2 is 2 cm above them. A head 3/5 palpable at station -2 is not engaged, which is why artificial rupture of the membranes carried a risk of cord prolapse.
focus: Intrapartum obstetric emergency: abnormal CTG and cord prolapse in labour
guide:
In Part 1, the examiner (as Sam) gives findings from the Exam findings only when the student says what they would examine. Part 1 is a rapid history and examination; if the student starts management, Sam acknowledges it, and it counts when the management is marked in Part 2. If the student has not examined vaginally by the end of Part 1, the vaginal examination items are not ticked, and the reassessment in Part 2 tells them the cord is felt. The maternal observations and the reassessment are snapshots and are the same whatever was started in Part 1. A high-performing candidate gets the key history quickly (oxytocin recently increased, recent artificial rupture with a high head, epidural top-up, no pain or bleeding, no uterine scar), checks the signal, maternal observations and contractions, and asks for a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse, finding the pulsating cord. In Part 2 they describe the CTG accurately, identify tachysystole and hypotension, diagnose cord prolapse, and give their management in order: call for help, stop oxytocin, elevate the presenting part and keep it elevated, position head-down, avoid handling the cord, correct hypotension, and category 1 caesarean with no delay, while talking to Mrs Costa. They explain LOA and station accurately.

A borderline candidate finds the abnormal CTG but misses one of the first measures (usually stopping oxytocin or the vaginal examination), or does not call for help early. They may identify the cord prolapse but not keep the presenting part elevated, forget the head-down position, delay the caesarean behind other steps, or not explain what is happening to the woman.
patient:
Role: One role-player plays Mrs Maria Costa, a 29-year-old woman in bed on the birth suite with a working epidural; she is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. The examiner plays the midwife, Sam. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the student says what they would examine. If the student starts management in Part 1, Sam says "Noted"; management is marked in Part 2.

Opening line (Sam): "The baby's heart rate has dropped and it is not coming back up. Can you help me while the registrar comes?"

History from Sam (give only when asked):

  • Induction of labour at 39 weeks and 4 days, at Mrs Costa's request after discussion with the obstetric team, because she was anxious about going overdue. Uncomplicated pregnancy, single baby, head down.
  • Oxytocin infusion running since this morning. The rate was last increased 30 minutes ago.
  • Membranes ruptured artificially 20 minutes ago, with clear fluid. The vaginal examination then showed 5 cm dilatation with the head high, at station -2, LOA.
  • Epidural working well. A top-up was given 15 minutes ago; her blood pressure before it was 110/65.
  • The CTG was normal until about 10 minutes ago (the trace is handed over in Part 2). The contractions have become very frequent.
  • Group B streptococcus negative. The placenta was not low on the morphology scan.

History from Mrs Costa (give only when asked):

  • This is your second baby. Your first was a normal vaginal birth at term, 3.4 kg, with no complications. You have never had a caesarean or other operation on your womb.
  • No pain between contractions apart from pressure, and no bleeding. You felt the baby moving earlier today.
  • No medical problems. No medicines apart from the drip and the epidural. No allergies. You last ate toast about 6 hours ago.
  • Your husband is sitting beside you and is frightened.

Behaviour: you are anxious and ask, "Why has everyone rushed in? Is the baby okay?" If you are told clearly and kindly, you agree to any examination or change of position. If the student does not explain, ask "What are you doing?" and become more distressed. With help, you can get onto all fours or into a knee-chest position despite the epidural.

In Part 2: if the student explains that you need an urgent caesarean, say: "Okay, just please get my baby out safely. Can my husband come with me?"
points: For an abnormal CTG, call for help early, alongside the first measures: reposition, correct hypotension, stop oxytocin for hyperstimulation, check temperature, check signal and perform a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse.
In cord prolapse, elevate the presenting part, position head-down, handle the cord minimally and proceed to category 1 caesarean without delay.
LOA describes position: the occiput (denominator) lies left and anterior in the maternal pelvis.

Tachysystole on oxytocin and hypotension after an epidural top-up are common, correctable causes of an abnormal CTG, but a sudden prolonged deceleration soon after artificial rupture of the membranes with a high head needs a vaginal examination for cord prolapse.
After a cord prolapse birth, the neonatal team attends, paired cord blood gases are taken and the woman and her partner are offered a debrief.

stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement on the birth suite of a metropolitan hospital. You are in the room with the midwife, Sam, who is caring for Mrs Maria Costa, a 29-year-old woman at 39 weeks and 4 days who is having an induction of labour. Sam is worried about the CTG and asks you to help while the obstetric registrar is paged. The registrar is on the way.
tasks: Take a rapid focused history from Sam and Mrs Costa and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you the CTG, Mrs Costa's observations and a reassessment. Interpret them, then outline your immediate management approach, including what you say to Mrs Costa, and give your safety netting (5 minutes).
title: Abnormal CTG on the birth suite

part2.lead: Here is the CTG, Mrs Costa's observations, and a reassessment 3 minutes later.

handover.label: CTG
handover.result:
Intrapartum CTG (external ultrasound transducer and tocodynamometer) at 39 weeks 4 days, oxytocin infusion running, epidural in place. Paper speed 1 cm/min. The last 30 minutes reviewed at 11:45.

FeatureFinding
SignalGood, no loss of contact; fetal heart distinct from the maternal pulse (105/min)
Baseline rate140 bpm until 11:42
Baseline variabilityNormal, about 10 bpm, until 11:42
AccelerationsPresent until 11:30; none since
DecelerationsNone until 11:42. From 11:42, a prolonged deceleration starting with a contraction, down to 70 bpm and lasting 3 minutes so far, not recovering
Uterine activityFrom about 11:35, 6 contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting about 90 seconds, with little rest between them
handover.model:
Read (RANZCOG features): a good signal. Until 11:42 the baseline was 140 bpm with variability of about 10 bpm, both normal. Two abnormal features: excessive uterine activity, with 6 contractions in 10 minutes (tachysystole is more than 5) lasting about 90 seconds with little relaxation, on an oxytocin infusion; and a prolonged deceleration (more than 90 seconds) to 70 bpm, now 3 minutes long and not recovering.

Meaning: an abnormal CTG with a feature likely to be associated with fetal compromise. A deep prolonged deceleration of 3 minutes needs urgent obstetric review and preparation to expedite birth, and a sudden deceleration soon after artificial rupture of the membranes with a high head is cord prolapse until a vaginal examination shows otherwise. The tachysystole and the maternal hypotension both reduce placental blood flow and add to it.

What it changes: call for help now (registrar, obstetric emergency call), stop the oxytocin, move her off her back, correct the hypotension and examine vaginally for the cord; consider terbutaline if contractions continue. Fetal blood sampling has no place in a prolonged deceleration that does not recover: birth is expedited.

handover.label: Maternal observations
handover.result: BP 110/65 at 11:28, before the epidural top-up at 11:30.
handover.model:
Read: BP 84/50 at 11:45 and 86/50 at 11:48, against 110/65 before the epidural top-up 15 minutes earlier, with a maternal tachycardia of 105 to 108 (above the 10 to 20 beat rise of pregnancy). RR, SpO2 and temperature (37.1 °C) are normal and she is alert.

Meaning: hypotension from the epidural top-up (sympathetic block, worse lying semi-supine), which lowers uterine and placental blood flow and adds to the fall in the fetal heart rate, but the cord prolapse is the main cause. No fever, so no sign of chorioamnionitis or sepsis; a temperature of 38 °C or above would need a sepsis screen.

What it changes: an IV fluid bolus, keeping her off her back (the knee-chest or left lateral head-down position helps), and anaesthetic review for a vasopressor if the BP does not respond. The anaesthetist needs this before the category 1 caesarean.

rows.note: Registrar still a few minutes away

handover.label: Reassessment 3 minutes later
handover.result:
CTG at 11:48: the fetal heart rate has recovered only slowly, to about 100 bpm, and has not returned to the baseline of 140 bpm. Variability reduced, 3 to 5 bpm. No accelerations. Contractions continue.

Vaginal examination: the cord is still felt pulsating below the presenting part. Cervix 5 cm, vertex at station -2.

The registrar is still a few minutes away.
handover.model:
Read: 6 minutes after the deceleration began, the fetal heart has recovered only to about 100 bpm, still 40 bpm below its baseline, with reduced variability (3 to 5 bpm, an abnormal feature) and no accelerations. The cord is still pulsating below a high presenting part, with the cervix 5 cm.

Meaning: umbilical cord prolapse with continuing cord compression and fetal compromise. The first measures have not restored the trace, and at 5 cm a vaginal birth is not close.

What it changes: a category 1 caesarean, aiming for birth as fast as is safely possible: keep the fingers elevating the presenting part and keep her knee-chest or head-down until the baby is born, handle the cord as little as possible, fill the bladder only if transfer or delay is expected, and make sure the emergency call brings the anaesthetist, theatre and the neonatal team. Nothing waits for the registrar to arrive.

ask: What does the CTG show, and what do the observations and the reassessment tell you?
What is the diagnosis, what has contributed to the change in the trace, and what does LOA at station -2 mean?
What would you do first, and what next? Tell Mrs Costa what is happening.
What happens after the birth, for Mrs Costa and her baby?
